chapter: Preface (p. xiii) vs Ch 2 §2.1 (p. 15) vs Ch 4 §4.3 (p. 72)
evidence: Preface, PDF p. 19: "In the book's convention (Ch. 2, 4), TTFTe2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill + first decode step, where tokenization/transfer counts as one combined term." | Ch 2, PDF p. 35: "Timing convention (used throughout the book). We attribute the first sampled token to prefill: prefill = processing the prompt + sampling token 1, and decode = the per-token loop that begins with token 1 as its first input and produces token 2 onward." | Ch 4, PDF p. 92: "TTFT_e2e convention (used throughout): TTFTe2e = retrieval+admission/queue+tokenization/transfer + prefill."
issue: Three different TTFT_e2e formulas for the same named convention. The Preface adds '+ first decode step'; Ch 4 omits it; Ch 2's own prefill/decode attribution ('prefill = processing the prompt + sampling token 1') means the first decode step — the forward pass whose input is token 1 and whose output is token 2 — occurs strictly AFTER the first token is available and therefore after TTFT. The Preface's formula double-counts a step that lies outside the TTFT interval under the book's stated convention, and it also contradicts Ch 4's restatement of the same convention two chapters later. This is load-bearing: the canonical 1.2 s TTFT budget and the 'prefill ~1.08 s' residual are derived from this decomposition.
fix_instruction: Pick one TTFT_e2e formula and state it once in the Preface, then make Ch 2 §2.1 and Ch 4 §4.3 quote it verbatim. Under the book's own convention (first token sampled inside prefill), TTFT_e2e must NOT contain '+ first decode step'; if the intent is to include the decode step that consumes token 1, say so explicitly and reconcile it with the 'prefill includes sampling token 1' rule, because the two cannot both hold.

chapter: Preface — The Architect's Evidence Discipline (p. xi)
evidence: PDF p. 17: "ILLUSTRATIVE — a chosen scenario input or worked example ([canonical scenario] or [ILLUSTRATIVE], paired with ASSUMPTION or DERIVED), on the book's teaching geometry, to be re-derived per deployment." | "Provenance (Axis 1) records where the number came from: ... [ILLUSTRATIVE] a non-canonical worked-example or scenario input chosen to make a calculation concrete, ..." | "The third axis — measurement status (ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED, or UNMEASURED where the stage is not yet determined) — rides with that pair or stands alone."
issue: [ILLUSTRATIVE] is defined twice, on two different axes, with two different meanings. On Axis 1 (provenance) it means 'a non-canonical worked-example or scenario input chosen to make a calculation concrete'. On Axis 3 (measurement status) it means 'a chosen scenario input or worked example ... on the book's teaching geometry'. The Axis-3 definition explicitly includes the canonical scenario, which Axis 1 explicitly excludes from [ILLUSTRATIVE]. Every [ILLUSTRATIVE]-tagged cell in the book (Ch 3 Tables 3-2/3-3, Ch 5 Table 5-2, Ch 7 Figs 7.1/7.4/7.5/7.6/7.7/7.8) is therefore ambiguous: the reader cannot tell from the tag whether the number is canonical or non-canonical, or whether the tag is provenance or measurement status.
fix_instruction: Rename one of the two. Keep [ILLUSTRATIVE] as the Axis-1 provenance tag (non-canonical worked example) and rename the Axis-3 measurement-status member to something distinct (e.g. MODELLED / SCENARIO-DERIVED), then add one line in the Preface's evidence-boundary panel stating which axis the surviving [ILLUSTRATIVE] belongs to. Apply the rename to the Axis-3 list only.

evidence: Fig 6.1, PDF p. 123: "Workload metrics | rps · token profile · concurrency | Resource metrics | HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · memory pressure | Serving metrics | TTFT · TPOT · goodput ... queue depth: scheduler state, not a serving metric" | §6.1.1, PDF p. 121: "1. This is exactly the separation Ch 4 §4.3 insists on ('Concurrent users ≠ concurrent requests').

evidence: Fig 7.7, PDF p. 160: "in-flight ≈ KV budget ÷ KV per request | ≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5 → ~17 requests" | Ch 4, PDF p. 90: "Requests in flight ≠ KV-resident sequences. A request in the queue, or one whose prefill is not yet admitted, is 'in flight' from the user's perspective but does not yet hold a KV slot. In-flight concurrency upper-bounds the KV-concurrency the system must serve, but the KV budget is sized by the number of resident active sequences"
issue: The figure labels the KV-slot count as 'in-flight' and equates it with KV-budget ÷ KV-per-request. Ch 4 makes the opposite distinction a named common mistake and states that the KV budget is sized by resident sequences, not by in-flight requests. The label therefore uses, in the one diagram a reader is most likely to screenshot, precisely the term the book warns is wrong; the same distinction is silently respected in Ch 17's ⌈344/17⌉ screen, where 344 is the Little's-Law in-flight figure being divided by resident-slot capacity.

evidence: PDF p. 47: "Two residency bases, named: at the pre-generation 9.2K-input point the request's KV is 24.1 GB, so total resident is ~228 GB (140 GB weights + ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve + 24.1 GB KV); at the end-of-generation 9.5K resident basis the same host holds ~229 GB (140 + 64 + 24.9 GB — the figure Ch 7 Fig 7.8 uses)."
issue: Within a single sentence, 'resident' carries two different meanings: 'total resident' = the aggregate memory footprint of weights + reserve + KV on the host, while '9.5K resident basis' = the token-count basis (input + output tokens) used for KV slot sizing. The book elsewhere (Ch 4 Table 4-2 'the resident slot-counting basis, §4.6') uses 'resident' only in the token-basis sense, so the two senses are actively in tension. The figure the sentence points at (Ch 7 Fig 7.8) labels the same quantities 'used' and 'KV', not 'resident'.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the sentence to use one word for each concept — e.g. 'the host footprint is ~228 GB' versus 'the 9.5K-token slot-counting basis gives ~229 GB' — and keep 'resident basis' reserved for the token-count sense as in Ch 4 Table 4-2.

evidence: PDF p. 125: "Deploying a higher-throughput configuration can reduce goodput: goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction, so a throughput increase helps goodput only if the compliant fraction holds. ... Scenario A [ILLUSTRATIVE]: the extra 20 tok/s are produced, but they land in the tail that misses the SLO, so goodput does not grow. Raw throughput is up 40%; goodput (tokens that met the SLO) is effectively unchanged in this case" | PDF p. 126: "Scenario B [ILLUSTRATIVE]: if the compliant fraction falls from 96% to 94%, goodput is 50×0.96 = 48 vs 70×0.94 = 65.8 — it rises despite the p95 breach."
issue: Neither scenario supports the section's opening claim that a higher-throughput configuration 'can reduce goodput': Scenario A leaves goodput unchanged and Scenario B raises it. Worse, Scenario A's 'unchanged' result requires a specific and unstated compliant fraction: to hold goodput at 50 × 0.96 = 48 with raw rate 70, the compliant fraction must fall from 96% to 48 ÷ 70 = 68.6%, a 27-point collapse — not the 2-point drop used in Scenario B. The two scenarios are therefore not comparable as presented, and the reader is left with 'goodput does not grow' for a reason that is never shown and is far more extreme than the adjacent scenario implies.
fix_instruction: Either add a Scenario C that actually reduces goodput (state the compliant fraction that makes 70 × f < 50 × 0.96, i.e. f < 68.6%), or retitle the section to the claim the evidence supports ('a p95 breach does not determine goodput') and state Scenario A's implied compliant fraction (0.96 → 0.686) explicitly so the two scenarios are comparable.

evidence: PDF p. 126 (Fig 6.2 caption): "Reproducibility: the sample p99 of 1.33 s is contingent on exactly 100 stragglers in this draw — with 101 of 10,000 the interpolated sample p99 is 5.0 s, while the population p99 is 5.0 s in either case; reproduce with the stated stream definition (99% log-normal, median 0.8 s, + 1% at 5.0 s, N = 10,000)." | PDF p. 124: "The plotted stream is a synthetic sample of N = 10,000 requests — 99% drawn from a log-normal with median 0.8 s, 1% a straggler cluster at 5.0 s — and the percentiles are read by linear interpolation on the sorted sample."
issue: The 'stated stream definition' that the caption offers for reproduction omits the log-normal's dispersion parameter (σ or equivalent). A log-normal is fully specified by two parameters; only the median (0.8 s) is given, so the quoted p90 (0.94 s), p95 (0.99 s) and mean (0.85 s) cannot be regenerated — a wide range of σ values produce a median-0.8 log-normal with very different means and p95s. (Back-solving from the figure's own p95 ≈ 0.99 s implies σ ≈ 0.13, which is nowhere stated.) The p99 knife-edge is carefully documented, but the parameter that actually fixes the body of the distribution is missing.
fix_instruction: Add the dispersion parameter to the stated definition in both places — e.g. '99% log-normal, median 0.8 s, σ ≈ 0.13, + 1% at 5.0 s, N = 10,000' — and state the seed or generator, so the p50/p90/p95/mean and the p99 knife-edge are both reproducible.

evidence: Ch 8, PDF p. 173: "The utilization-only (ρ = 1, no 95% N+1 term) screen is total = ⌈N ÷ 0.7⌉ — 30 for KV-only, 32 for case (ii) — and is reported as a floor, not a deployment count." | Ch 4, PDF p. 103: "the book's provisioning policy, which multiplies the independent ρ = 0.95 as well and then adds the N−1 reserve"
issue: ρ is used for two different factors in the fleet-sizing rule: Ch 4 assigns ρ = 0.95 to the availability/utilization derating and calls the 0.70 the 'u' target, while Ch 8 writes '(ρ = 1, no 95% N+1 term)' — using ρ = 1 to mean 'the 0.95 factor omitted' while simultaneously applying 0.7. Ch 8 also bundles '95%' and 'N+1' into one phrase, although Ch 8's own policy sentence two paragraphs earlier separates them: 'total = ⌈N ÷ (0.7 × 0.95)⌉ ... and working = total − 1 (one host held for failure reserve)'. The spare is '+1 host', not 'N+1', and it is not the same term as the 95% factor.
fix_instruction: Use one symbol per factor across both chapters (e.g. u = 0.70 utilization target, ρ = 0.95 availability derating, plus a separate '+1 spare'), and rewrite the Ch 8 clause as 'the utilization-only screen (no ρ derating, no spare) is total = ⌈N ÷ 0.7⌉'.

evidence: PDF p. 140: "3×H100 total VRAM | 240 GB | [DERIVED] 165 GB < 240 GB | fits 3×H100 at 9.2K? | passes aggregate bytes only; TP=3 placement not established | 164.1 GB < 240 GB, but tensor parallelism shards attention heads, not the hidden dim ..." — while the two adjacent rows read "2×H100 total VRAM | 160 GB | [1P: NVIDIA H100 spec]" and "8×H100 total VRAM | 640 GB | [1P: NVIDIA H100 spec]"

fix_instruction: Change the derivation cell to '3 × 80 GB [1P][DERIVED]' (or '[1P: NVIDIA H100 spec] × 3'), tag it [1P][DERIVED] to match the sibling rows' provenance, and remove the duplicated fit comparison — it belongs only in the 'fits 3×H100 at 9.2K?' row, where it should read 164.1 GB < 240 GB for consistency with the 2×H100 and 8×H100 rows.

evidence: PDF p. 85: "GQA/MQA and sparse attention shrink the KV constant several-fold (Ch 7), so ~2.62 MB/token is a deliberate upper bound and Appendix A §7's Fig A.2 (vendor-relative KV/compute ratios) is its deliberate relaxation, not a correction."
issue: The Preface states the cross-reference convention explicitly: 'Section cross-references use the § chapter.section form: a bare § N.M refers to chapter N, section M'. 'Appendix A §7' violates that form — an appendix subsection must be cited as § A.7 (the book's own apparatus uses 'A.3', 'A.6' elsewhere, e.g. 'Appendix A, A.6 carries a boxed 2026-09-27 capability probe'). The bare '§7' also invites the wrong reading — Ch 7 is a different chapter, whose §7 is 'Memory Is the First Constraint'.
fix_instruction: Rewrite as 'Appendix A § A.7's Fig A.2' (or simply 'Appendix A's Fig A.2, vendor-relative KV/compute ratios'), and sweep the body for any other bare '§N' used against an appendix.

fix_instruction: Add the same qualifier to the Ch 2 Table 2-1 derivation cell — 'weight-only intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte (omits the ~24 GB KV write; ~7,850 FLOP/byte including it, Ch 8)' — so the two chapters' disclosures match.

evidence: p.132: 'The architecture is memory-sane at the 10 rps design point but was never compute-sized for it' with '(deployed host count H = 1)'. The book's own arithmetic: 10 rps → ~86 in-flight (Ch 4 p.90) vs 17 KV slots/host (436 ÷ 24.9, Ch 7 p.139), requiring ~6 hosts at 10 rps (Ch 4 p.98-99: 'the KV-residency screen (86 in-flight ÷ 17 slots = 5.06) is the binding bound and raises this to ~6 hosts').
issue: The mini-case premise contradicts the book's own KV-residency/concurrency arithmetic: one host is not 'memory-sane' at 10 rps (86 in-flight vs 17 resident slots; the same paragraph computes a 4.7× prefill oversubscription at baseline, so SLOs were already breached before lunch). It commits exactly the single-request-fit vs concurrent-capacity conflation that Ch 7's fit note (p.139: 'this residency check answers a single-request question... It says nothing yet about how many such requests fit concurrently') warns against.
fix_instruction: Reword the premise to 'the deployment passed the single-request residency check (≈165 GB < 640 GB) but was never sized for concurrency or compute', or set the deployed fleet to the canonical ~6 hosts and keep the lunch-peak failure.

evidence: p.133: 'an H-host fleet sized at 10 rps with H ≈ 5 would be ~3.7× oversubscribed at the peak' and 'hosts were raised from H = 1 to H = 19 (the Ch 8 case (i) screen), which took the peak from 18.6× to 51.6 ÷ (19 × 2.77) ≈ 1.0×'. The book's binding 10-rps fleet is 6 hosts (Ch 4 p.98-99), and the 40-rps peak KV floor is 21 hosts (Ch 8 p.169: 'the full-utilization KV-residency floor is ~21 hosts (Ch 17's floor-17 screen)'); 19 × 17 = 323 resident slots < 344 in-flight at the 40 rps peak.
issue: The mini-case sizes fleets by the prefill-compute screen only and ignores the KV-residency screen the book itself applies: (a) 'H ≈ 5' should be 6 at 10 rps (peak oversubscription ~3.1×, not ~3.7×); (b) the remediation to H = 19 leaves ~21 of 344 peak in-flight requests unresidentsble (≈6% > 5%), so the claimed outcome 'p95 TTFT is back under 2 s' cannot hold under the book's own model (Ch 6 p.125 itself shows queuing pushes p95 past 2 s).
fix_instruction: Use the binding screens (6 hosts at 10 rps; 21 at 40 rps) in the mini-case, or state explicitly that it tracks the compute screen only and that KV-residency sizing (Ch 17) adds hosts on top before the SLO-restoration claim.
